entry.title: Zakura RPC listener bound beyond loopback with cookie authentication disabled exposes unbounded history-scan and address-query methods to unauthenticated remote callers, allowing node resource exhaustion and denial of service.
entry.content:
An AI audit bot found a medium-severity denial-of-service issue in Zakura’s zakurad RPC interface. When the listener is exposed beyond loopback and cookie authentication is disabled, remote anonymous callers can invoke methods that perform effectively unbounded chain scans or collect large address-query results in memory. Default installations are unaffected because they use loopback binding and cookie authentication.

The vulnerable code

In crates/zakura-rpc/src/server.rs, the RPC server assembly conditionally creates authentication middleware. When conf.enable_cookie_auth is false, line 134 constructs the layer without a cookie:

That is dangerous when combined with a non-loopback listener because configuration validation permits the RPC interface to become remotely reachable without credentials.

The getnetworksolps implementation in crates/zakura-rpc/src/methods.rs converts the caller’s num_blocks directly to a traversal count around line 2838:

No maximum is enforced. The solution_rate backend in crates/zakura-state/src/service/read/difficulty.rs then uses that value around line 103:

Address queries have a similar scaling problem. The build_height_range function in crates/zakura-rpc/src/methods.rs, around line 4729, interprets an omitted or zero end height as the current chain height:

Consequently, get_address_tx_ids can request the entire indexed history. Its address count is also unrestricted, and transparent_tx_ids in crates/zakura-state/src/service/read/address/tx_id.rs collects all matching results before returning them.

Why the code is wrong

The first assumption is that operators will preserve the safe defaults. That fails when an operator deliberately disables cookie authentication while binding RPC to 0.0.0.0, ::, or another externally reachable address. Zakura accepts this combination instead of rejecting it.

The second assumption is that RPC callers will choose reasonable workloads. getnetworksolps validates negative values but does not cap positive ones. A value such as 2000000000 therefore reaches the ancestor iterator, which walks until either the requested count or available chain history is exhausted.

The third assumption is that address queries remain naturally small. In reality, callers control the address set and height range, while the backend has no unified limit on work or returned data. Wide queries can consume substantial disk I/O and memory, especially when repeated concurrently.

How it plays out

An attacker first identifies a reachable Zakura RPC port configured without cookie authentication. They send a small JSON-RPC request containing an enormous num_blocks, causing a scan across all available ancestors. They can alternate this with getaddresstxids requests containing many addresses and full-chain height ranges.

Repeated or parallel calls compete with synchronization, peer handling, state access, and mempool processing for CPU, memory, and storage bandwidth. RPC latency rises, and the node may become unavailable. The impact is availability loss, not fund theft or consensus corruption, and its severity depends on chain size, indexing, hardware, and concurrency.

The fix

Operationally, RPC should remain bound to loopback or an authenticated private network, with cookie authentication enabled. Firewalls and authenticated reverse proxies add useful protection but should not replace application authentication.

Zakura should reject non-loopback listeners when authentication is disabled, unless an explicit high-risk override is provided. getnetworksolps also needs a documented maximum and a fast validation failure:

Address methods should cap address count, height span, result size, and concurrent expensive requests. Large results should be paginated rather than accumulated without a memory budget. Regression tests should cover IPv4 and IPv6 wildcard listeners, oversized parameters, bounded results, and responsiveness under concurrent RPC load.

entry.title: Zakura's opt-in health endpoint rate-limits only connection arrivals, not connection lifetime or active-connection count, so an unauthenticated client can hold incomplete or keep-alive HTTP connections below the arrival threshold and accumulate sockets and per-connection tasks across rate-limit windows until file descriptors are exhausted, failing legitimate health checks and pressuring process-wide resources.
entry.content:
Zakura’s opt-in health server has a medium-severity resource-exhaustion vulnerability in zakurad. Its rate limiter restricts connection arrivals, but does not bound connection lifetime or the number of active connections. A reachable, unauthenticated client can therefore retain enough slow HTTP connections to exhaust process-wide file descriptors, disrupt health checks and other node networking, and trigger a CPU- and log-heavy accept-error loop.

The vulnerable code

The issue is in run_health_server at crates/zakurad/src/components/health.rs:308. The listener accepts a connection, applies a fixed-window arrival counter, and then spawns an independent task:

Lines 311-319 count accepted arrivals against MAX_RECENT_REQUESTS, which is 10,000 per five seconds. Lines 326-330 spawn serve_connection without a timeout or concurrency permit. Lines 332-334 immediately retry failed accepts without backoff.

The health configuration at crates/zakurad/src/components/health/config.rs:8-28 exposes listen_addr and readiness settings, but no header timeout, idle timeout, connection lifetime, or active-connection limit.

Why the code is wrong

The code treats arrival rate as if it also bounded retained work. That assumption fails whenever connections survive longer than the limiter’s five-second window.

  1. num_recent_requests tracks newly accepted sockets, not sockets that remain open.
  2. Once accepted, each socket moves into a detached tokio::spawn task and is no longer represented in the limiter.
  3. serve_connection has no application-configured header-read, idle, keep-alive, or total-lifetime deadline.
  4. No semaphore limits how many connection tasks can coexist.
  5. When descriptor exhaustion makes accept() return EMFILE, the error branch logs and retries immediately, adding CPU use and warning-log volume to the original outage.

The endpoint must be enabled and reachable for this to matter. A loopback-only listener or a correctly constrained reverse proxy substantially reduces exposure.

How it plays out

An attacker sends partial requests such as:

By omitting the final blank line, the client leaves HTTP header parsing incomplete. It opens connections below 10,000 arrivals per five seconds, so every window appears compliant, while keeping earlier sockets alive.

Over multiple windows, active sockets and Tokio tasks continue accumulating. Eventually the process reaches its file-descriptor limit. New /healthy and /ready probes fail, potentially causing orchestrators or load balancers to remove or restart the node. Because descriptors are process-wide, peer and RPC sockets may also be affected. The exact threshold and operational response depend on the deployment and were not established by source review alone.

The fix

The listener needs controls over retained work as well as arrivals. It should acquire a global semaphore permit before spawning a connection task and immediately close the socket when no permit is available. The permit must remain owned by the task and be released on completion, timeout, error, or disconnect.

serve_connection should also be subject to short header-read, idle, keep-alive, and total-lifetime deadlines, using Hyper’s supported controls and tokio::time::timeout where appropriate. Optional per-source connection quotas would further limit one client’s share.

Repeated accept failures need bounded exponential backoff, particularly for EMFILE, instead of immediate retry. Configuration should expose values such as header_timeout, idle_timeout, and max_connections.

Operationally, the health listener should remain on loopback or a restricted management network. A reverse proxy can provide immediate connection limits and deadlines, but application-level bounds are still necessary to cover direct exposure, proxy bypass, and configuration drift.

entry.title: Zakura's TLS-enabled RPC listener spawns an unbounded Tokio task per accepted TCP connection and awaits the TLS handshake with no deadline or global connection limit, allowing unauthenticated remote clients to exhaust file descriptors and task capacity before authentication ever runs, denying service to legitimate RPC clients and potentially crashing the RPC service or node.
entry.content:
An AI audit of Zakura found a medium-severity availability vulnerability in the optional TLS RPC listener. When TLS RPC is enabled, unauthenticated clients can leave arbitrarily many handshakes pending, consuming sockets and Tokio tasks before cookie authentication runs. Independent verification confirmed the vulnerable control flow in the source, although the exact exhaustion threshold and any propagation into full node shutdown remain deployment-dependent.

The vulnerable code

The issue is in crates/zakura-rpc/src/server.rs, in the TLS branch of the RPC server setup beginning around line 150. The accept loop creates a new task for every accepted socket:

Three lines are central. Around line 186, tokio::spawn allocates independent work for every connection without first acquiring a permit. Around line 188, acceptor.accept(socket).await has no deadline. At lines 174-177, any listener.accept() error is returned from the RPC task, including an EMFILE error caused by descriptor exhaustion.

There is also no matching resource control in crates/zakura-rpc/src/config/rpc.rs: TlsConfig only exposes certificate and key files, with no handshake timeout or connection limit.

Why the code is wrong

The implementation assumes that accepted peers will either complete TLS promptly or fail and disconnect. TCP does not provide that guarantee. A client can establish a connection, send no ClientHello, and remain connected.

That broken assumption produces four related problems:

  1. Task creation is unbounded. Each accepted socket immediately reaches tokio::spawn. There is no global semaphore or per-source quota limiting concurrent connection work.

  2. The TLS wait is unbounded. acceptor.accept(socket).await can remain pending while a silent or deliberately slow client retains a file descriptor, a Tokio task, and TLS state.

  3. Shutdown is observed too late. The accept loop watches stop_handle, but an already spawned task does not race its handshake against shutdown. The stopped signal only affects serving after TLS succeeds.

  4. Resource pressure becomes a fatal error. Once the process runs out of descriptors, listener.accept() may return EMFILE. The loop propagates that error instead of applying backoff and recovering, terminating the RPC task.

Cookie authentication and request-level rate limiting do not address any of these points because no RPC request exists yet.

How it plays out

The vulnerable deployment must have TLS RPC enabled and reachable without a firewall or front proxy imposing its own limits. An attacker repeatedly opens TCP connections and withholds all or part of the TLS handshake.

The attack requires neither an RPC cookie nor a client certificate. Its confirmed impact is loss of RPC availability. Depending on process limits and Zakura’s service supervision, exhaustion may also crash the RPC service or contribute to broader node shutdown. Loopback-only binding, strict firewalling, or a correctly limited TLS proxy substantially reduces exposure.

The fix

The server needs both a time bound and an admission bound. A handshake deadline closes silent connections:

A timeout alone is insufficient because new connections can arrive faster than old ones expire. The listener should acquire a global semaphore permit before spawning connection work and immediately close sockets when the budget is exhausted. Per-source limits can prevent one address from occupying the entire allowance.

Pending handshakes should also observe shutdown directly:

Finally, temporary accept failures such as EMFILE should trigger bounded backoff, logging, and controlled recovery rather than immediate RPC-task termination. TlsConfig should expose handshake_timeout and connection-limit settings, backed by regression tests for silent peers, quota enforcement, shutdown cancellation, overload recovery, and successful legitimate RPC access under pressure.
